extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, and empirical researchers learning logic of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging when observed regularities count as laws, how to detect causal relations vs chance, and how to apply averaging and probability to eliminate chance in empirical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical law (definition and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed uniformities not resolved into ultimate laws; 'empirical laws' are derivative uniformities the derivation of which has not been traced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which they have been found true by observation; they cannot safely be extended beyond those limits until either confirmed by the Method of Difference or explained deductively (accounted for a priori). The text emphasizes that many results obtained by the Method of Agreement (simple observation without experiment) must be considered empirical laws until so confirmed or explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement only ascertains the whole of the circumstances common to all cases in which a phenomenon is produced and therefore never by itself proves causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the aggregate of common circumstances includes causes and collateral uniformities, the Method of Agreement affords no means of determining which uniformities are laws of causation and which are merely derivative; thus conclusions from this method remain empirical laws unless confirmed by Method of Difference or deductive explanation. (Original phrasing: 'the utmost that the Method of Agreement can do is, to ascertain the whole of the circumstances common to all cases ... The method affords no means of determining which of these uniformities are laws of causation...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of derivative law: evidence of intermediate links
rubrics_metrics.description: If between antecedent a and consequent b there is evidence (or reason to surmise) of some intermediate phenomenon x, the law a causes b is likely derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence or suspected existence of intermediate links implies that the observed law is resolvable into at least two laws (a causes x; x causes b). Example: chemical formation of water — we observe gases mixing and water resulting, but infer intervening corpuscular processes, so chemical laws are derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of derivative law: extremely complex antecedent (composition of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent is an extremely complex phenomenon composed of many elements, its observed effects are likely compounded from effects of its parts, indicating the law is derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the ordinary case is that effects of the whole are made up of effects of parts, sequences from complex antecedents are probably resolvable into simpler laws. Examples: weight (sum of particles' weights) and meteorological antecedents (atmospheric column composed of air and aqueous vapor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative authority of derivative vs ultimate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws (and uniformities not known to be laws of causation) possess less generality and certainty than the simpler ultimate laws from which they are resolvable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until empirical uniformities are explained deductively or resolved into causes, they 'have not attained the highest degree of certainty' and are 'unfit to be relied on beyond the limits of time, place, and circumstance' in which they were observed. Use greater caution in extending such laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of chance (casual coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance is best described as coincidence from which we have no ground to infer a uniformity — two or more phenomena conjoined but not related by causation or common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is incorrect to say a phenomenon is produced by chance; rather, phenomena may be casually conjoined (neither cause and effect nor effects of the same cause). Recurrence of a coincidence does not by itself prove it is the result of a law; frequency only matters when it exceeds what chance (given the separate frequencies of the phenomena) would account for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of causes problem (limits on inference from coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a phenomenon may have many possible causes, observing the same antecedent A with consequent a in several cases does not by itself prove causation—the phenomenon might have been produced by different causes in different instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The uncertainty from plurality of causes diminishes with the multiplication of consistent instances pointing to A, but one must consider the possibility that differing elements in instances produced the effect. This is the characteristic imperfection of the Method of Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for assessing coincidence vs chance via marginal frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether a conjunction of A and B is due to law rather than chance, compare the observed co-occurrence with the frequency expected from the separate frequencies of A and B (i.e., expected co-occurrence if independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: if A occurs in 1/2 of cases and B in 1/3, then if independent they'd co-occur in 1/6. If observed co-occurrence is greater than 1/6 (or if A occurs in larger proportion where B is than where B is not), infer some causal connection; if less, infer repugnance or counteracting causes. Also illustrated with fixed stars (always present) and wind/rain example (account for differing base rates of winds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes (constant vs variable causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect is produced by a constant cause modified by many variable causes, the observed result in single instances is a mixture of constant and casual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because variable modifying causes are different and uncontrollable, one cannot isolate the constant cause by single observation. The recommended method is to perform many trials holding the constant cause A fixed and examine the distribution/average of results to infer the effect of A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of chance by repeated trials and averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: When A's action is blended with indeterminate modifying causes, make many trials preserving A; the mean of results estimates the effect of A, while deviations are due to chance (variable causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test of sufficiency is when increasing the number of trials does not materially alter the average. Application: eliminate unavoidable experimental errors by averaging; assume errors on either side will balance when no systematic bias exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of residual phenomenon by eliminating chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Small constant effects that escape notice individually can be uncovered by averaging many observations until the mean stabilizes at a non-zero residual, indicating a constant cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: detecting loaded dice (small persistent bias), diurnal variation of the barometer (small average difference by hour). Conclude existence and quantify a constant cause when further trials leave the average materially unchanged and non-zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing significance with limited samples — role of theory of probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the long-run expected frequency, one must ask what deviation from that average can reasonably occur by chance in smaller samples; this question belongs to the doctrine of chances (theory of probabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that deciding how large a deviation from expected frequency is credible by chance requires probabilistic analysis; it is not sufficient to rely only on qualitative frequency reasoning when sample sizes are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's conception of probability (equally possible cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability is measured by reducing events to a number of equally possible cases and taking the ratio of favorable cases to all possible cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements per Laplace: (1) among the events some one (and only one) must happen; (2) we must be 'equally undecided' as to which will happen. The passage also records a critique that empirical frequency evidence is needed to justify treating cases as equally probable.
